planting.note: Set divisions in spring into circumneutral to slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil, since this species comes from base-rich rock and woodland soils and dislikes strongly acidic ground.

directions: Carolina alumroot is a woodland species split out from the more widespread Heuchera americana, found only in a narrow range across Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina where it grows on base-rich rock outcrops, basic dikes, and calcium-enriched upland forest soils. Its basal rosette of lobed, marbled leaves sends up airy, leafy flowering stems that can reach well over two feet in late spring, taller than the compact mound typical of garden coral bells. In cultivation it prefers the same circumneutral to slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil of its native habitat and resents strongly acidic or waterlogged conditions. Give it dappled shade beneath deciduous trees and divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS), UNC Chapel Hill Herbarium

planting.note: Tuck divisions into shaded rock crevices or sharply drained, gritty soil in spring, replicating the thin mineral soils of its native rocky ledges.

directions: New Mexico alumroot is a regional native of mountains in New Mexico and adjacent Arizona, growing directly from cracks and ledges of shaded rock outcrops at mid to upper elevations. Its compact basal foliage sends up slender flowering stems in early summer carrying small, cream to yellow-green bells, a quieter floral display than the showier red-flowered Heuchera species sold in nurseries. Because it evolved on thin, mineral soils wedged among rocks, it performs best in a shaded rock garden or crevice planting with sharp drainage rather than a rich, consistently moist border. Established clumps can be divided in spring to propagate or renew older plantings.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Wedge divisions into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil among rocks in spring, since this high-elevation species rots quickly in rich, moisture-retentive ground.

directions: Wooton's alumroot is a narrow endemic of a handful of mountain ranges in south-central New Mexico, including the Sacramento Mountains, Sierra Blanca, and Capitan Mountains, where it roots into talus slopes and rock outcrops from pinon-juniper woodland up into subalpine conifer forest. It is distinguished from other alumroots sharing its range by pure white petals, carried on wiry stems above broad, heart-shaped basal leaves from early summer into early fall. Thick, persistent rhizomes let it survive for years wedged into rock crevices with minimal soil, so a well-drained rock garden setting mimicking that lean, gritty substrate suits it better than a conventional perennial bed. Give it light shade and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil that encourages crown rot.
sources: New Mexico Rare Plants Technical Council (nmrareplants.unm.edu)

planting.note: Set nursery-propagated divisions into sharply drained, rocky soil in spring, choosing a cool, shaded crevice that mimics its high-elevation boulder-field habitat.

directions: Parish's alumroot, also called Mill Creek alumroot, is a California endemic restricted to high-elevation rock and boulder fields of the San Bernardino Mountains, where it is tracked as a rare plant by the California Native Plant Society. Its kidney-shaped, lobed leaves form a low spreading patch among rocks, from which wiry stems lift dense clusters of small salmon-pink, bell-shaped flowers. As an alpine-to-subalpine crevice dweller, it needs sharply drained, mineral soil and the cool root run of a rock garden rather than a typical humus-rich shade bed. Because wild populations are limited, gardeners growing it should rely on nursery-propagated material rather than wild-collected plants.
sources: California Native Plant Society Rare Plant Program (rareplants.cnps.org)
